news.title: Fed up voters 'wiped' almost every 'scandal-plagued' candidate from the map
news.description: Puck reporter Leigh Ann Caldwell reports next year’s Democrat-led Ethics committees may have their hands full scrutinizing President Donald Trump and his shady business deals with no-bid contractors — among his other corruption allegations — but the committees ‘naughty list’ just got a whole lot lighter. “Washington may be giving thanks for the near-total decimation of this cycle’s crop of scandal-plagued candidates, almost all of whom lost their elections in November — potentially giving next year’s Ethics committees a much-needed reprieve,” said Caldwell. On the Democratic side, Maine’s Graham Platner didn’t get far into the general election before dropping out and getting swapped for Democrat Troy Jackson, after numerous scandals hit the press. Critics had fretted that Platner’s departure was an open door for Republican Maine Senate incumbent Susan Collins to stroll back into the Senate, but it just didn’t pan out that way in the wave election that swept Republicans out to sea. North Carolina GOP Rep. Chuck Edwards similarly abandoned his bid for reelection in the wake of a House Ethics Committee report finding that he’d intimately harassed two staffers. Caldwell suggested that scandal-plagued Texas senatorial candidate Ken Paxton could have taken a lesson from Edwards and dropped out, but didn’t. This gave his Democratic challenger James Talarico an effortless jaunt into the Texas U.S. Senate seat. “Elsewhere, the Hill will soon bid adieu to Rep. Mike Collins, who lost the Georgia Senate race to Jon Ossoff shortly before the House Ethics Committee found ‘substantial evidence’ that his office accepted ‘improper voluntary service,’” said Caldwell. Ohio Rep. Max Miller, meanwhile, faced domestic abuse allegations and an Ethics investigation, before losing to Democrat Brian Poindexter. Although Caldwell added that Poindexter himself will probably be another box to check in an upcoming committee investigation with his own allegations of intimate harassment. “Laurie Buckhout lost to Democratic Rep. Don Davis after she bet on her own race in prediction markets. Extremist YouTuber turned extremist Republican House candidate Brandon Herrera lost his race to Katy Padilla Stout in Texas. David Flippo, a Republican candidate who faced questions about his finances and expected an Ethics investigation for failing to submit financial disclosures as a candidate, lost his Nevada House race,” added Caldwell. “And, of course, Democratic Rep. Jimmy Gomez, a close friend of disgraced former congressman Eric Swalwell, lost to fellow Democrat Angela Gonzales-Torres after being accused of misconduct with a staffer from another office. Caldwell added, however, that there is an exception in Tennessee State Senator Brent Taylor, who narrowly beat his Democratic challenger — but only after the state’s Republican legislature gerrymandered 9th district, despite Taylor admitting that he’d sent unsolicited intimate photos to women as recently as 2021. He dismissed the act as “youthful indiscretions,” even though he’s pushing 60. “But overall, voters made clear this cycle that corruption was a dealbreaker,” said Caldwell, explaining that the “naughty list” got “wiped out.” “It appears that the Ethics Committee, which is among the worst assignments on the Hill, will have less work to do in the new year … for now.”

news.title: 'Over my dead body': Tensions boil over as Dems rush to save institution from Trump
news.description: Democrats pledged to defend the Smithsonian's independence after ProPublica reported draft plans for an overhaul of its American History museum. Rep. Chellie Pingree (D-ME), slated to lead the subcommittee that funds the Smithsonian, wrote to its Board of Regents on Tuesday, ProPublica reported. She told the outlet she would investigate and said the plans fit a broader pattern of White House interference. "No White House employee riding on the Metro gets to design a plan for what future exhibits look like," she said. The Smithsonian gets federal money but is governed by a 17-person Board of Regents that includes the chief justice, the vice president, members of Congress and private citizens. In recent months, Trump has put up signs outside the Smithsonian disclaiming their contents as political — a move that has been long sought by the Christian nationalist movement. But that could just be the beginning. ProPublica wrote that a commuter photographed a White House staffer's laptop and notes on a D.C. Metro train in late October, and that it verified the material. They showed a 25-item list of possible changes to the National Museum of American History, which the outlet said would amount to an unprecedented attempt to control its content and staff. It included firing top officials, a permanent exhibit called "The Riches of Our Western Civilization Inheritance," a Founders-focused K-12 curriculum and a "Colossus Statue" of George Washington. The staffer and White House didn't respond, and it was unclear how the plans were received inside. Smithsonian leader Lonnie Bunch told staff the list's purpose was unclear, but the institution was independent, per ProPublica. Sen. Alex Padilla (D-CA) said if he chaired the Rules Committee, it would protect the institution, which he said wasn't a federal agency. Fred Wellman, elected this month to represent St. Louis suburbs, wrote, "Over my dead body."
